# Introduction

This guide summarises the content and competencies for the six-week regression
section of STA2005S. It is intended to help you answer three questions:

1. What should I know?
2. What should I be able to do?
3. Where can I learn and practise it?

The main regression lecture notes, `NotesReg.pdf`, remain a key source
throughout and are not repeated under every week. The weekly slides, supporting
documents, question bank, tutorials and practicals should be used alongside
those notes.

::: {.callout-important title="How to use this guide"}
The guide is comprehensive, but it does not replace instructions given in
lectures or for a specific assessment. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you
should be able to explain, calculate, interpret and apply the listed material,
not merely recall definitions.
:::

## Weekly overview

| Week | Main theme | Central questions |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Foundations and the multivariate normal distribution | What is regression, what mathematical tools does it require, and how do normal random vectors behave under transformations? |
| 2 | The general linear model | How is the model formulated, how are its parameters estimated, and what are the distributions of the estimators? |
| 3 | Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests | How do we quantify uncertainty and perform inference for one or several linear combinations of regression coefficients? |
| 4 | ANOVA and model checking | How are categorical variables represented, how are nested models compared, and how do we assess whether a fitted model is credible? |
| 5 | Matching the model to the data | How can transformations and interactions improve the model, how do we predict and select variables, and why is OLS special? |
| 6 | Bootstrapping and principal components analysis | How can resampling support inference, and how can high-dimensional explanatory variables be represented more simply? |

# Week 1: Foundations

## Content

### The purpose and scope of regression

- Response and explanatory variables.
- Explanatory versus predictive aims.
- What regression adds beyond:
  - a correlation coefficient;
  - a two-sample $t$ test;
  - estimating an overall mean.
- Simple versus multiple linear regression.
- The broad regression workflow:
  - formulate the question;
  - explore the data;
  - specify and fit a model;
  - quantify uncertainty;
  - check the model;
  - interpret and communicate the result.
- The assumptions of a linear regression model and why each matters.

### Statistical distributions

- Moving between the normal, chi-squared, $t$ and $F$ distributions.
- Constructing chi-squared variables from independent standard normal variables.
- Constructing $t$ and $F$ variables from normal and chi-squared variables.
- Degrees of freedom and their role in the shapes and quantiles of these
  distributions.

### Linear algebra

- Dimensions, rows, columns and notation.
- Matrix addition, multiplication and transposition.
- Block matrices and block-matrix multiplication.
- Orthogonality and orthonormality.
- Trace and the cyclic trace property.
- Rank, full rank and linear dependence.
- Invertibility and conditions under which an inverse exists.
- Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
- Symmetric, positive-definite and idempotent matrices.
- Factorisations of symmetric matrices and properties of the eigenvalues of
  idempotent matrices.

### Multivariate normal distribution

- The univariate and multivariate normal density functions.
- Mean vector, variance-covariance matrix and marginal distributions.
- The moment-generating function of a multivariate normal random vector.
- Linear transformations of multivariate normal random vectors.
- Partitions and marginal distributions of multivariate normal random vectors.
- Quadratic forms:
  - using the inverse covariance matrix;
  - using a symmetric idempotent matrix;
  - the connection to the chi-squared distribution.

## Competencies

By the end of Week 1, you should be able to:

- explain when regression is useful and distinguish explanatory from predictive
  goals;
- identify the response, explanatory variables and sources of random
  variability in an applied problem;
- perform matrix calculations and keep track of dimensions;
- determine whether a matrix is symmetric, full rank, orthogonal,
  positive-definite or idempotent;
- use block matrices and eigenvalue properties in short proofs;
- state the parameters of a multivariate normal distribution;
- find the distribution of a linear transformation or partition of a
  multivariate normal random vector;
- derive or recognise chi-squared quadratic forms;
- reproduce the principal Week 1 proofs and adapt the same results in new
  derivations;
- use R to explore a response and its relationships with possible explanatory
  variables.

# Week 2: The general linear model

## Content

### Model formulation

- General linear model:

  $$
  \mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.
  $$

- Scalar, vector and matrix representations.
- Dimensions and roles of $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{X}$,
  $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$.
- Known quantities, unknown parameters and unobserved random variables.
- The fixed-design interpretation of $\mathbf{X}$.
- Mean and variance of $\mathbf{Y}$.
- Model assumptions:
  - linearity in the parameters;
  - zero conditional mean of the errors;
  - constant error variance;
  - uncorrelated errors;
  - normality where exact finite-sample inference requires it;
  - full column rank of $\mathbf{X}$;
  - more observations than estimated parameters.
- Recognising plausible violations in applied settings.
- Simple and multiple linear regression as special cases.

### Design matrices and model interpretation

- The intercept column.
- Constructing design matrices for numerical explanatory variables.
- Column ordering and its effect on the coefficient vector.
- Full column rank, collinearity and why
  $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ must exist.
- Interpreting a regression coefficient while holding other explanatory
  variables fixed.
- How variation and correlation among explanatory variables affect the
  variances and covariances of coefficient estimators.

### Estimating $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

- OLS in simple linear regression.
- OLS and maximum likelihood in the normal general linear model:

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  =(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}.
  $$

- Derivation and calculation of the estimator.
- Unbiasedness and variance-covariance matrix.
- Distribution:

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \sim
  N_k\left(
    \boldsymbol{\beta},
    \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \right).
  $$

- Distributions of single and multiple linear combinations:
  $\boldsymbol{\ell}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and
  $\mathbf{L}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.

### Estimating $\sigma^2$

- Maximum likelihood estimator of $\sigma^2$.
- Bias of the maximum likelihood estimator.
- Unbiased estimator
  $s^2=\mathrm{SSE}/(n-k)$.
- Distribution of $(n-k)s^2/\sigma^2$.
- Effect of the residual degrees of freedom on the precision of $s^2$.

### Fitted values and residuals

- Fitted values:
  $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.
- Residuals:
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=\mathbf{Y}-\hat{\mathbf{Y}}$.
- Errors versus residuals.
- Hat matrix
  $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'$.
- Residual-maker matrix $\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}$.
- Fitted values and residuals as projections.
- SSE, MSE and their relationship to $s^2$.

## Competencies

By the end of Week 2, you should be able to:

- translate an applied model between scalar, vector and matrix notation;
- identify known quantities, parameters, errors, responses and fitted values;
- construct a design matrix and state the dimensions of every model component;
- state the assumptions and explain likely violations;
- calculate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ from first principles;
- state when the OLS formula is well-defined;
- interpret individual regression coefficients precisely;
- calculate fitted values and residuals and distinguish residuals from errors;
- derive and use the distribution of
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and its linear combinations;
- calculate the maximum likelihood and unbiased estimators of $\sigma^2$;
- explain the bias of $\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ and the role of
  residual degrees of freedom;
- explain how the design matrix affects estimator precision.

# Week 3: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

## Content

### Foundations for inference

- Sampling variability and standard errors.
- Distribution of
  $\boldsymbol{\ell}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.
- Independence of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $s^2$.
- Why estimating $\sigma^2$ changes a normal pivot into a $t$ pivot.
- Degrees of freedom.
- Nominal versus empirical coverage.
- Conditions required for exact or approximately valid inference.

### Confidence intervals

- General confidence interval for
  $\boldsymbol{\ell}'\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
- Special cases:
  - an individual regression coefficient;
  - a difference between coefficients;
  - an arbitrary contrast;
  - a conditional mean response
    $\mathbf{x}_f'\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
- Calculation, interpretation and reporting.
- Interval width and its relationship to:
  - confidence level;
  - sample size and residual degrees of freedom;
  - $s^2$;
  - the design matrix;
  - the location of $\mathbf{x}_f$.
- Why a confidence interval is not a probability statement about a fixed
  parameter after the data have been observed.

### Hypothesis tests for one linear combination

- Null and alternative hypotheses for
  $\boldsymbol{\ell}'\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
- One-sided and two-sided alternatives.
- Derivation and calculation of the $t$ statistic.
- Critical-value and p-value approaches.
- General p-value formulae for one-sided and two-sided tests.
- Relationship between a two-sided test and a confidence interval.

### Hypothesis tests for several linear combinations

- Hypotheses of the form
  $\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{c}$.
- Derivation and calculation of the $F$ statistic.
- Special cases:
  - several specified coefficients;
  - all slope coefficients;
  - all coefficients, including the intercept;
  - arbitrary simultaneous contrasts.
- Why separate $t$ tests do not replace a joint test.

### Interpretation

- Statistical significance versus effect size and practical importance.
- What a large p-value does and does not imply.
- Distinguishing:
  - a precise estimate near zero;
  - an imprecise estimate compatible with important effects;
  - a statistically significant but negligible effect;
  - a large and practically important effect.
- The role of confidence intervals in communicating magnitude and precision.

## Competencies

By the end of Week 3, you should be able to:

- derive and calculate a confidence interval for any specified
  $\boldsymbol{\ell}'\boldsymbol{\beta}$;
- construct $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ from a substantive comparison or fitted-value
  question;
- state and test one-sided and two-sided hypotheses;
- calculate a test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value;
- construct $\mathbf{L}$ for a set of simultaneous restrictions;
- derive and apply the general $F$ test;
- explain nominal and empirical coverage and investigate coverage by
  simulation;
- use the $t$ rather than normal distribution when appropriate;
- interpret confidence intervals and p-values without confusing lack of
  evidence with evidence of no effect;
- report the estimated effect, uncertainty and test result in context.

# Week 4: ANOVA and model checking

## ANOVA and categorical variables

### Content

- One-way ANOVA:
  - model formulation;
  - group means and the overall mean;
  - between-group, within-group and total sums of squares;
  - degrees of freedom;
  - mean squares;
  - the $F=\mathrm{MSA}/\mathrm{MSE}$ statistic.
- ANOVA as a special case of the general linear model.
- Representing categorical variables:
  - indicator or dummy variables;
  - reference levels;
  - why an intercept plus one indicator for every level is not full rank;
  - alternative codings;
  - models without an intercept.
- Constructing and interpreting a design matrix containing numerical and
  categorical explanatory variables.
- Interpreting the intercept and category coefficients.
- The effect of centring or recoding a variable on coefficient
  interpretations.
- Confidence intervals and tests for:
  - one category difference;
  - a comparison between non-reference categories;
  - an average or other linear combination of effects;
  - the overall effect of a multi-level categorical variable.
- Reduced and full models.
- Nested-model $F$ test:

  $$
  F =
  \frac{(\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F)/(k_F-k_R)}
       {\mathrm{SSE}_F/(n-k_F)}.
  $$

- Relationship among:
  - the classical ANOVA $F$ test;
  - the general $\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ test;
  - `anova()` comparisons of nested models;
  - the overall $F$ statistic in `summary(lm(...))`.
- Sequential sums of squares and why order can matter in an ANOVA table.
- Partial effects in multiple regression and the sense in which regression
  treats each variable as if it entered last.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- calculate a one-way ANOVA table from first principles;
- translate an ANOVA model into regression notation;
- select a reference level and construct the corresponding design matrix;
- identify the reference level from model output;
- interpret coefficients under different codings;
- express substantive comparisons as linear hypotheses;
- construct reduced and full models for a question about one or more terms;
- calculate and interpret a nested-model $F$ test;
- identify the null hypothesis of the overall `summary(lm(...))` $F$ test;
- distinguish a single coefficient test from an overall test of a multi-level
  factor.

## Model fit, assumptions and influential observations

### Content

- Coefficient of determination:
  - formula using sums of squares;
  - interpretation and range;
  - relationship to
    $\operatorname{Cor}(\mathbf{Y},\hat{\mathbf{Y}})^2$;
  - why it cannot decrease when variables are added.
- Adjusted $R^2$:
  - formula;
  - motivation;
  - advantages and limitations.
- Revisiting the model assumptions:
  - correct mean structure and linearity;
  - constant variance;
  - independence;
  - normality;
  - adequate design and absence of exact collinearity.
- Graphical checks:
  - residuals versus fitted values;
  - residuals versus explanatory variables;
  - residual histogram or density;
  - normal Q-Q plot and its simulation band.
- Formal normality tests:
  - Shapiro-Wilk;
  - Kolmogorov-Smirnov;
  - null hypotheses, relative power, and limitations compared with graphical
    methods.
- Residual distribution:

  $$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
  =(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{Y},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})
  =\sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}).
  $$

- Internally and externally studentised residuals:
  - formulae;
  - motivation;
  - interpretation and useful thresholds.
- Leverage:
  - diagonal elements $h_{ii}$ of the hat matrix;
  - bounds, total and average leverage;
  - why high leverage is a property of the explanatory-variable values;
  - effect of leverage on fitted values and residual variance.
- Outlying, high-leverage and influential observations.
- Cook's distance:
  - purpose;
  - components;
  - interpretation and common threshold.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- calculate and interpret $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$;
- identify likely assumption violations from plots and applied descriptions;
- combine graphical and formal evidence without over-interpreting either;
- derive and use the variance of an individual residual;
- distinguish errors, raw residuals and studentised residuals;
- distinguish an outlier from a high-leverage or influential observation;
- calculate leverage, average leverage and studentised residuals;
- explain why residual variance decreases as leverage increases;
- identify potentially influential observations and recommend sensible
  follow-up rather than automatically deleting them;
- give an integrated judgement about whether a fitted model is adequate.

# Week 5: Matching the model to the data

## Transformations and additional model terms

### Content

- Why the original linear model may not match the data:
  - non-linearity;
  - non-constant variance;
  - skewness;
  - outliers;
  - missing effect modification.
- Transforming the response:
  - common log and square-root transformations;
  - linearising relationships;
  - stabilising variance;
  - reducing skewness and the impact of extreme observations;
  - consequences for every explanatory-variable relationship;
  - interpretation on the transformed and original scales.
- Transforming an explanatory variable:
  - log, square-root, exponential and square transformations;
  - correcting a specific non-linear relationship;
  - why this does not itself fix non-constant residual variance;
  - interpretation after transforming $X$.
- Introducing new explanatory variables:
  - polynomial terms;
  - discretised versions of a numerical variable;
  - interactions.
- Interactions between a numerical and a categorical explanatory variable:
  - model formula;
  - design matrix;
  - fitted lines for each group;
  - group-specific intercepts and slopes;
  - differences between groups at a specified value of $X$;
  - two-level and multi-level factors.
- Tests involving interactions:
  - whether slopes differ across groups;
  - whether $X$ has an effect within a specified group;
  - whether $X$ has an effect in any group;
  - whether groups differ at a specified value of $X$;
  - whether a factor has any effect through either intercepts or slopes.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- diagnose which aspect of a model a transformation is intended to address;
- decide whether transforming $Y$, transforming an $X$, or adding model terms
  is the more targeted response;
- interpret coefficients on transformed scales and describe the corresponding
  relationship on the original scale;
- construct the design matrix for polynomial and interaction models;
- calculate and plot fitted values for every level of an interacting factor;
- interpret main effects in the presence of an interaction;
- calculate group-specific slopes and between-group differences;
- express each substantive interaction question as one or several linear
  restrictions and choose a $t$ or $F$ test accordingly;
- re-check the model after modifying its structure.

## Prediction, variable selection and model performance

### Content

- Conditional mean versus an individual future response.
- Confidence interval for a mean response versus prediction interval for a new
  observation.
- Sources of variability in each interval.
- Prediction interval:

  $$
  \hat{Y}_f
  \pm
  t_{n-k}^{1-\alpha/2}
  s\sqrt{
    1+\mathbf{x}_f'
    (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
    \mathbf{x}_f
  }.
  $$

- Why prediction intervals are wider than confidence intervals.
- What happens to each interval as sample size grows.
- Why interval bands widen away from the centre of the observed design.
- Motivation for variable selection:
  - interpretation;
  - cost of measurement;
  - prediction accuracy;
  - bias-variance trade-off.
- Why exhaustive search is often infeasible.
- Algorithms:
  - forward selection;
  - backward elimination;
  - stepwise selection.
- Selection criteria:
  - AIC;
  - BIC;
  - adjusted $R^2$;
  - balancing fit against model complexity.
- How the AIC and BIC penalties differ as sample size changes.
- Limitations of greedy selection algorithms.
- Why ordinary p-values are not trustworthy after data-driven variable
  selection without accounting for the selection process.
- Training and test data:
  - evaluating prediction on unseen observations;
  - optimism of training error;
  - trade-off in choosing the split size;
  - uncertainty in the fitted model versus uncertainty in estimated test error.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- derive and calculate a prediction interval;
- explain every source of uncertainty in a confidence or prediction interval;
- choose the interval appropriate to an applied decision;
- describe forward, backward and stepwise selection and identify when each can
  or cannot be run;
- calculate and compare AIC and BIC values;
- explain why a criterion may favour a larger or smaller model;
- critique inferential claims made after model selection;
- design a training-test split and explain its competing sources of
  uncertainty;
- evaluate predictive performance on unseen data.

## Gauss-Markov theorem

### Content

- Statement and assumptions of the theorem.
- Meaning of each word in BLUE:
  - best;
  - linear;
  - unbiased;
  - estimator.
- Proof that OLS has the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators.
- Normality is not required for the Gauss-Markov result.
- Difference between:
  - OLS being BLUE;
  - OLS being maximum likelihood;
  - exact normal-theory confidence intervals and tests being valid.
- Consequences of:
  - omitted variables correlated with included variables;
  - non-linearity in the parameters;
  - non-constant variance;
  - correlated errors;
  - biased estimators with smaller variance.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- state the Gauss-Markov theorem precisely;
- identify which assumptions are needed and which are not;
- explain the comparison class implicit in the word "best";
- reproduce the proof and explain why the added covariance term is
  non-negative;
- determine whether the theorem applies to a proposed model;
- distinguish low variance from low mean-squared error when bias is present;
- explain why satisfying the theorem does not establish that a model is
  scientifically adequate.

# Week 6: Bootstrapping and principal components analysis

## Bootstrapping

### Content

- Sampling distributions and why they are needed for inference.
- Limitations of normal and $t$ approximations when the sampling distribution
  is skewed or otherwise poorly approximated.
- The central idea of the non-parametric bootstrap:
  - treat the empirical distribution as an estimate of the population
    distribution;
  - sample observations with replacement;
  - keep each bootstrap sample the same size as the original sample;
  - recompute the statistic for many bootstrap samples.
- Why sampling with replacement is essential.
- Bootstrap estimate of a sampling distribution and standard error.
- Bootstrap confidence intervals:
  - percentile interval;
  - interval using a bootstrap standard error and a theoretical $t$ quantile;
  - bootstrap-$t$ interval.
- Which intervals can be asymmetric and where the asymmetry arises.
- Comparing bootstrap methods with ordinary normal and $t$ intervals.
- Strengths and limitations:
  - fewer parametric assumptions;
  - dependence on the observed sample being representative;
  - difficulty with very small samples, dependent observations or inappropriate
    resampling units;
  - simulation error and the number of bootstrap repetitions.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- explain sampling with replacement and construct a bootstrap sample;
- distinguish a data distribution from a statistic's sampling distribution;
- describe the bootstrap algorithm in words, notation and R;
- estimate a bootstrap standard error;
- calculate or interpret percentile, bootstrap-standard-error and bootstrap-$t$
  intervals;
- identify which interval methods allow asymmetry;
- explain when a bootstrap method may improve on a theoretical approximation;
- identify settings in which a naive bootstrap would be unreliable.

## Principal components analysis

### Content

- Purposes of PCA:
  - dimensionality reduction;
  - visualisation;
  - pattern recognition;
  - noise reduction;
  - reducing collinearity among derived explanatory variables.
- Centring and, where appropriate, standardising the original variables.
- Covariance-matrix versus correlation-matrix PCA.
- Definition of a principal component as a linear combination of the original
  variables.
- Loading vectors and the unit-length constraint.
- Principal-component scores.
- Variance-maximising objective and orthogonality constraints.
- Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix as loading vectors.
- Eigenvalues as component variances.
- Ordering of components and why components are uncorrelated.
- Total variance and proportion of variance explained:

  $$
  \operatorname{PVE}_j
  =\frac{\lambda_j}{\sum_{r=1}^p\lambda_r},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{CPVE}_m
  =\frac{\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j}{\sum_{r=1}^p\lambda_r}.
  $$

- Choosing the number of components:
  - scree plot and elbow;
  - cumulative proportion of variance explained;
  - interpretability and the aim of the analysis.
- Interpreting loadings:
  - magnitude;
  - sign;
  - contrasts and shared patterns among variables;
  - arbitrary reversal of a component's sign.
- Consequences of a covariance matrix that is not full rank.
- Regression using principal-component scores and the resulting coefficient
  correlations.
- Costs and limitations:
  - information loss;
  - difficult interpretation;
  - sensitivity to scale;
  - high variance need not mean high relevance to a response.
- Reading and interpreting the main output of `prcomp()`.

### Competencies

You should be able to:

- explain why PCA is used and when standardisation is necessary;
- calculate a covariance matrix and its eigendecomposition;
- identify the loading vector and variance of each component;
- calculate principal-component scores for specified observations;
- prove or explain why component variances are eigenvalues and components are
  uncorrelated;
- calculate total, individual and cumulative proportions of variance
  explained;
- draw and interpret a scree plot;
- motivate the number of components retained using more than one criterion;
- interpret a component from its loadings while recognising sign ambiguity;
- explain the effect of rank deficiency;
- relate PCA to regression with correlated explanatory variables;
- critique the claim that the last components are necessarily irrelevant.

# Statistical computing and applied analysis

The practical strand is cumulative. A later assessment may require earlier R
and data-analysis skills even when its statistical topic comes from a later
week.

| Practical stage | Competencies |
|---|---|
| Data preparation and exploration | Load and inspect data; calculate summaries; distinguish numerical, nominal and ordinal variables; create histograms, densities, boxplots, scatterplots and pairwise plots; identify skewness, outliers and possible collinearity. |
| Model formulation and fitting | Simulate data; create factors with appropriate levels; construct model and design matrices; fit simple, multiple, categorical, transformed and interaction models; calculate OLS estimates manually. |
| Inference | Extract model components; calculate standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values and nested-model tests; distinguish individual and simultaneous hypotheses. |
| Programming foundations | Work with vectors and matrices; write `for` loops; use conditions and `if`, `else` and `ifelse`; distinguish scalar and element-wise logical operators; write and debug functions. |
| Simulation | Estimate coverage and power; keep fixed and random quantities distinct; repeat an analysis reproducibly; summarise and plot simulation results. |
| Model assessment | Calculate ANOVA components; obtain fitted values and residual diagnostics; identify outliers, leverage and influence; compare training and test performance. |
| Communication | State the analytical goal; justify model choices; interpret effects in context; report uncertainty; distinguish statistical from practical importance; present reproducible code and clear tables and figures. |

The [previous practicals](../_reference/eval/2025/) and
[previous assignment](../_reference/eval/2025/AssignmentRegQuestions.qmd)
show how these competencies can be combined in longer applied questions.

# Final revision checklist

Before an assessment, check that you can do each of the following without
depending on a memorised example:

- translate a substantive question into a model and one or more hypotheses;
- construct the relevant design row, contrast vector or contrast matrix;
- calculate an estimate, standard error, interval or test statistic;
- state the assumptions behind the calculation;
- interpret the result in the units and context of the problem;
- identify what the result does not establish;
- use diagnostic evidence to assess the model;
- connect the mathematics to the corresponding R output;
- reproduce the required proofs and adapt the underlying results to a new
  derivation.
